idiom_name: class User extends BaseEntity + @Entity/@Column, static find/create/save and instance remove
implementation_notes: TypeORM supports the pattern explicitly: active-record entities extend BaseEntity and the model itself carries the operations (User.create, user.save, User.find, user.remove), with @Entity/@PrimaryGeneratedColumn/@Column decorators and reflect-metadata providing the mapping. What replaces the classic structure is the base class plus decorator metadata - no mapper class is written - and the entity only works after a DataSource has been initialised, because the static methods resolve against it. Choose it for small TypeScript services already on TypeORM; the data-mapper mode (repository per entity) is the same framework's alternative and the safer choice for larger domains.
pitfalls: Static BaseEntity calls run against the globally initialised DataSource: tests or apps that create several data sources get undefined behaviour unless every call goes through the right connection.
Decorators need experimentalDecorators and reflect-metadata in tsconfig/bootstrapping; missing either turns mapping errors into runtime surprises rather than compile errors.
save() persists the whole entity, so an object assembled from a request body overwrites columns that were never loaded.

variants.name: MikroORM entity extending BaseEntity (unit-of-work backed)
variants.idiom_name: class Book extends BaseEntity + em.find/flush (wrap() API on the instance)
variants.implementation_notes: MikroORM offers the same surface with a different engine: entities extend BaseEntity to expose the wrap() API on the instance (isInitialized, init, toObject), while persistence runs through EntityManager.persist/flush over an identity map and change-set computation - a loaded entity is managed automatically, so setting a property and flushing is enough to issue the UPDATE. What replaces the classic structure is the unit of work behind an active-record-looking object; choose it when you want record-style ergonomics without giving up cross-entity consistency, and expect the mapping rules (cascade, identity map) to be explicit.
pitfalls: Change tracking only sees managed entities: an instance created with new outside persist()/find() is not flushed, so mutations on it are silently lost.
One flush writes every tracked change at once, so an exception rolls back more than the statement you were thinking about - scope the EntityManager per request.
Entity definitions are patched at metadata discovery time: entities are only usable after MikroORM.init(), which bites in unit tests that import entities without initialising the ORM.
